title: Leg 58 — Split Rock to Rawlins
subtitle: Beaver Rim, Sweetwater country, Split Rock and Rawlins
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. We are leaving Lander and heading east across Beaver Rim into the broad Sweetwater country, then on toward Split Rock before turning south for Rawlins. This route crosses a landscape that once guided emigrant wagons, Pony Express riders and telegraph lines, but it also carries much newer stories of uranium boomtowns, railroad expansion, oil refining and frontier justice. Split Rock will be the major visual landmark of the flight, with its gunsight notch off the right side of our eastbound pass. I'll stay quiet while you taxi and depart. Once you're airborne and settled, say Trip continue.

waypoints.name: Split Rock North Pass
viewingNotes: Split Rock lies to the right of the eastbound pass.
The historic Sweetwater travel corridor spreads across the open country below.

blocks.title: Leaving Lander
blocks.spokenLabel: Lander and the Wind River Basin
blocks.text: We are leaving Lander behind and heading east across the southern edge of the Wind River Basin. The high country around Lander gives way surprisingly quickly to long open distances, sagebrush and layered rims. That change in scale is part of what makes central Wyoming look so different from the mountain corridors we have been flying lately.

blocks.title: Beaver Rim ahead
blocks.text: Beaver Rim forms the southern margin of the Wind River Basin and the northern edge of the Sweetwater Plateau. From the air it reads less like a single cliff than a long geologic step across the landscape, exposing thick stacks of sedimentary rock laid down during the Eocene, Oligocene and Miocene.

blocks.title: A long record in the rocks
blocks.text: The rocks along Beaver Rim preserve a surprisingly long environmental history. Ancient river deposits, floodplains, volcanic debris and lake sediments are stacked together here, and fossil finds in these formations include early mammals such as oreodonts, camels and other animals from a much warmer Wyoming than the one below us today.

blocks.title: The scale of the interior
blocks.text: This is a good stretch to notice how empty central Wyoming can feel from the air. Roads and ranch tracks may be visible for miles while settlements nearly disappear. That openness shaped both the old emigrant routes and the twentieth-century mining towns we will encounter farther east.

blocks.title: Onto the Sweetwater Plateau
blocks.text: East of Beaver Rim we are moving into the broad Sweetwater country, a landscape of low uplands, granite ridges and open sage. The Sweetwater River itself became one of the great guide lines of western migration because it offered travelers a comparatively gradual route toward South Pass.

blocks.title: A migration corridor on the ground
blocks.text: Between about 1840 and 1869, roughly half a million emigrants followed the great overland trail system toward Oregon, California and the Great Salt Lake Valley. Most people did not ride comfortably in their wagons; they walked beside them for much of the journey, saving wagon space and animals' strength for supplies and the sick.

blocks.title: The same corridor at a very different speed
blocks.text: The Pony Express later used much of this same trail corridor. Its Wyoming route linked a chain of stations across the state, including Split Rock and several Sweetwater stations. The service lasted only from 1860 into 1861, but its relay system turned a journey measured in months into mail delivery measured in days.

blocks.title: Jeffrey City comes into the story
blocks.text: Near this part of the route is Jeffrey City, one of Wyoming's starkest boom-and-bust stories. It began as a tiny roadside place called Home on the Range, then uranium discoveries transformed it during the Cold War. By 1980 the population had grown to more than four thousand. When the uranium market collapsed and the Split Rock mill shut down, most residents left within only a few years, leaving rows of modern buildings in what feels more like a recently abandoned suburb than an old western ghost town.

blocks.title: Wyoming's first uranium mill
blocks.text: The industrial side of the Jeffrey City story centered on the Split Rock uranium mill, built in 1957. It was Wyoming's first uranium mill and eventually processed about eight million tons of ore before closing in the early 1980s. For a generation, nuclear policy in Washington and uranium prices on world markets could determine whether this remote patch of Wyoming was booming or emptying out.

blocks.title: Following the Sweetwater corridor
blocks.text: The historic trails here generally followed the Sweetwater River westward toward South Pass. We are flying the opposite direction, but the geography still explains the route: water, comparatively gentle grades and a chain of unmistakable landmarks made this one of the most practical wagon corridors through central Wyoming.

blocks.title: What the trail actually felt like
blocks.text: The famous trail names can make the journey sound organized, but day to day it was mostly dust, weather, livestock, broken equipment and repetition. Disease killed far more emigrants than dramatic frontier violence did. Camps formed and dissolved constantly, and the same landmarks that look picturesque from the air were often practical checks that told exhausted travelers they were still on course.

blocks.title: Split Rock comes into view
blocks.text: Split Rock should now be becoming the obvious landmark ahead and to the right. Its gunsight-shaped notch rises about a thousand feet above the sagebrush plain. Westbound emigrants could see it for two days or more, and some wrote that they steered toward the cleft with almost compass-like confidence.

blocks.title: A landmark, station and communications stop
blocks.text: Split Rock was more than a visual marker. The trail corridor beneath it carried Oregon, California and Mormon emigrants, and in the early 1860s the nearby Split Rock Station served the Pony Express, stage traffic and the telegraph. So in one small area you can see several generations of western transportation layered together: wagons, horses, stagecoaches and wire.

blocks.title: The Split Rock pass
blocks.text: As we make the north-side pass, look off the right side for the notch itself and the granite mass rising above the plain. This is the kind of landmark that works especially well from the air: isolated enough to be unmistakable, but connected directly to the travel corridor spread out below it.

blocks.title: Leaving the emigrant landmark behind
blocks.text: Split Rock is beginning to fall behind as we turn south. The old emigrant trail continues west from here rather than following us toward Rawlins, so the historical story below shifts from wagon migration toward railroads, mining and energy.

blocks.title: Toward the Great Divide country
blocks.text: This part of Wyoming sits among broad interior basins separated by low divides and isolated ridges. Water does not always follow the simple east-versus-west pattern people associate with the Continental Divide; nearby closed basins can trap drainage internally instead of sending it all the way to an ocean.

blocks.title: A county shaped by energy booms
blocks.text: As we approach Carbon County, the economy has repeatedly risen and fallen with resources beneath the ground. Coal helped give the county its name, oil refining became a major industry, and uranium joined the mix in the twentieth century. The result is a landscape where tiny communities can have industrial histories far larger than their present populations suggest.

blocks.title: Parco became Sinclair
blocks.text: East of Rawlins sits the refinery town of Sinclair. It began in the 1920s as Parco, named from the initials of Producers and Refiners Corporation. The company built not only a refinery but a planned town with Spanish Colonial-style architecture, a central plaza and community facilities. After Sinclair acquired the operation, the town itself took the Sinclair name.

blocks.title: Rawlins ahead
blocks.text: Rawlins is coming into the broader basin ahead. Unlike the trail landmarks behind us, this city's growth was tied closely to the Union Pacific railroad and to its role as a regional service center in south-central Wyoming.

blocks.title: How Rawlins got its name
blocks.text: Rawlins traces its name to General John A. Rawlins, who was traveling with a railroad survey party in 1867. After scouts found a clear spring, Rawlins reportedly said that if anything were ever named for him, he hoped it would be a spring of water. The place became Rawlins Springs, and eventually simply Rawlins.

blocks.title: A railroad city in the high desert
blocks.text: The Union Pacific made Rawlins a division point, bringing railroad workers, freight traffic and the rough social world that followed the transcontinental line. Carbon County itself was created in 1868, and Rawlins later became the county seat.

blocks.title: The old state penitentiary
blocks.text: One of Rawlins' best-known landmarks is the old Wyoming Frontier Prison. Construction began in the territorial era, but money and weather delayed the opening until 1901. Its first cell block had no running water or electricity. The prison operated for about eighty years, and today it is a museum that still includes the cell blocks, gallows and gas chamber.

blocks.title: The strangest Rawlins outlaw story
blocks.text: Rawlins also owns one of the grimmer outlaw stories in the West. Train robber George 'Big Nose' Parrott was lynched here in 1881 after trying to escape jail. A local doctor, John Osborne, later had shoes made from Parrott's skin and reportedly wore them when he was inaugurated governor of Wyoming. The shoes are now displayed at the Carbon County Museum.

blocks.title: The prison became a movie set
blocks.text: The old penitentiary gained another strange chapter after it closed. In 1987 it was used as the location for the horror film Prison, one of Viggo Mortensen's early movie roles. Soon afterward the complex was preserved as a historic site instead of being lost to redevelopment.

blocks.title: Rawlins Municipal Airport
blocks.text: Rawlins Municipal Airport is ahead now. The city sits at roughly sixty-eight hundred feet above sea level, surrounded by the same open high-desert country that has shaped everything from wagon routes to railroads and energy towns on today's flight.
